## Introduction

R makes it remarkably easy to fit a multivariate linear model. You don't need a special
function. You just give `lm()` a matrix of responses instead of a single one:

```{r}
#| label: fit
fit <- lm(cbind(mpg, qsec) ~ hp + wt, data = mtcars)
class(fit)
```

<!--
mtcars is just for the hook: two responses, fuel economy and quarter-mile time.
A better-motivated example (Rohwer? iris? NeuroCog?) can take over in the package
sections. Or use one dataset throughout?
-->

The result is an object of class `"mlm"` that *also* inherits from `"lm"`. That second
class is a promise, or at least a hope: anything that works for a linear model should work
here too. So, as you would for any regression, you ask for the diagnostic plots:

```{r}
#| label: plot-fails
#| error: true
plot(fit)
```

Well, that's honest, at least. Other functions fail less gracefully. Several old friends from
the `car` package stop with messages that tell you nothing about why:

```{r}
#| label: car-fails
#| error: true
car::avPlots(fit)
car::vif(fit)
```

The more interesting cases are the ones that *don't* fail. `cooks.distance()` runs without a
murmur and gives you a Cook's D for each case, separately for each response:

```{r}
#| label: cooks-quiet
head(cooks.distance(fit), 4)
```

That's two univariate answers to what was a multivariate question: which cases have an undue
influence on the model as a whole? `summary(fit)` does the same thing, returning a list of
separate regression summaries, one per response, as if you'd called `lm()` twice. Nothing
warns you that the correlation between the responses, which is the whole point of fitting
them together, has dropped out of the analysis.

In short, the multivariate linear model is easy to fit and hard to see. @fig-techniques puts
this in a wider frame. It classifies the familiar linear-model methods by the number and kind
of predictors and responses. For one response ($q = 1$), we have a rich toolkit of graphical
methods: added-variable plots, influence plots, effect plots and the rest. For several
quantitative responses ($q > 1$), the methods are just as well developed on the statistical
side (multivariate regression, MANOVA, canonical correlation), but the graphics have been
thin. Mostly, the results arrive as tables of multivariate test statistics.

![Techniques for linear models, classified by the number of predictors ($p$) and responses
($q$), and whether these are quantitative or discrete. The $q > 1$ columns are where
graphical methods have been thin. *Source*: [Visualizing Multivariate Data and Models in
R](https://friendly.github.io/Vis-MLM-book), Figure 6.1.](figures/techniques-table.png){#fig-techniques width="90%" fig-alt="A table of linear-model techniques. Rows: predictors, quantitative or discrete, with p = 1 or p > 1. Columns: responses, quantitative or discrete, with q = 1 or q > 1. For quantitative responses, simple and multiple regression, t-test and ANOVA (q = 1) generalize to multivariate regression, canonical and partial correlation, Hotelling T-squared and MANOVA (q > 1). For discrete responses, logistic regression, chi-square, discriminant analysis, logit and loglinear models."}

## One more dimension

Why should this be so hard? The statistics of the multivariate linear model have been
settled for more than half a century. The trouble is more mundane, and I think it's worth
naming, because it explains nearly every problem I've run into.

When the response goes from a vector **y** to a matrix **Y**, every object the model produces
gains a dimension:

* a **scalar becomes a vector, or a matrix**. The residual variance $\sigma^2$ becomes a
  $q \times q$ covariance matrix $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$.
* a **vector becomes a matrix**. The coefficients $\mathbf{b}$ become a $p \times q$ matrix
  $\mathbf{B}$, and the residuals become an $n \times q$ matrix.
* a **matrix becomes a 3-way array**, or a list of matrices. A table of confidence intervals
  for the coefficients ($p \times 2$) becomes $p \times 2 \times q$. The standard error of each
  fitted value becomes a $q \times q$ matrix, one for every case.

@fig-dimension-ladder shows this ladder for a model with $p = 3$ coefficients and $q = 2$
responses.

![Going from `lm` to `mlm`, every object gains a dimension. Blue cells are what a univariate
model gives you; orange cells are added by the second response. The residual for a case
becomes a vector, the coefficient vector becomes a matrix, and the table of confidence
intervals becomes a 3-way array.](figures/dimension-ladder.png){#fig-dimension-ladder width="75%" fig-alt="A three-row diagram. Left column, lm with one response: a single cell for the residual e_i, a column of three cells for the coefficients b, and a 3 by 2 grid for their confidence intervals. Right column, mlm with q responses: each object gains orange cells along a new dimension, becoming a 1 by 2 vector, a 3 by 2 matrix B, and a 3 by 2 by 2 array drawn as two stacked layers."}

<!-- Drawn by R/dimension-ladder.R (run from this folder). Possible additions: a fourth
rung for sigma^2 -> Sigma (scalar -> matrix, skipping a rung), or se.fit. -->

That extra dimension shows up first in what a function *returns*, and then in every method that
has to consume it: `print()`, `summary()`, `confint()`, `predict()`, and of course `plot()`.
Code written for one shape is handed the next one up, and it has to do *something*.

Base R takes several different approaches. Sometimes it simply returns the bigger object:
`coef(fit)` is the $3 \times 2$ matrix you'd expect. Sometimes it **flattens** the extra
dimension away. `confint()` strings the responses and coefficients together into one long
list of intervals:

```{r}
#| label: confint-flat
confint(fit)
```

The `broom` package does much the same thing in tidy form, stacking the responses in a
long data frame with a `response` column. That's perfectly convenient for a table, but in both
cases the answers for `mpg` and `qsec` sit side by side as if they had nothing to do with
each other.

And sometimes R just **refuses**:

```{r}
#| label: predict-refuses
#| error: true
predict(fit, newdata = mtcars[1:2, ], se.fit = TRUE)
```

I have some sympathy for that last one. For a univariate model, the standard error of a
predicted value is a single number, and a confidence interval is a pair of numbers, `lwr` and
`upr`. For an `mlm`, the uncertainty of each predicted point is a $q \times q$ covariance
matrix, and the natural confidence region is an *ellipse* (an ellipsoid when $q > 2$) around
it. What should `predict()` return? How should it print? There's no column in
`cbind(fit, lwr, upr)` for an ellipse.

<!--
predict.mlm() is an unfinished item in heplots (dev/pred.mlm.R returns an n x q x 3
array). Mention here briefly, or save it for "What's still missing"? I'd keep a
one-sentence pointer here and the details at the end.
-->

So here's the argument of this post, in a nutshell:

::: {.thesis}
> A good multivariate extension isn't just "run the univariate method $q$ times". It has to
> decide what to do with the extra dimension: find the matrix that plays the role of the
> scalar, and then find a way to see it. Most often, as it turns out, that way is an ellipse.
:::

<!--
That's the thesis line. Alternative endings for that last sentence:

  - tie to Elliptical Insights (Friendly, Monette & Fox, 2013) here or later.
-->

## Filling in the gaps

Over the past twenty years or so I've been filling these gaps, one package at a time, often
with John Fox and Georges Monette:

<!-- CHECK: co-authors per package, and approximate start dates (from NEWS/DESCRIPTION).
     Is a personal-history thread wanted here, or keep it impersonal? -->

* [**heplots**](https://friendly.github.io/heplots/) shows multivariate hypothesis tests as
  ellipses: the HE plot.
* [**candisc**](https://friendly.github.io/candisc/) finds the low-dimensional view in which
  those tests are easiest to see.
* [**mvinfluence**](https://friendly.github.io/mvinfluence/) generalizes leverage and Cook's
  distance to multivariate models.
* `heplots::robmlm()` fits a robust version, downweighting cases with large residuals.
* [**genridge**](https://friendly.github.io/genridge/), my package for visualizing ridge
  regression, is now (in its development version) learning to handle a matrix of responses.

<!-- verify the pkgdown URLs before publishing -->

Each one is a case of the same problem: deciding what the extra dimension means, for the
statistics and for the software. The sections below take them in turn.

## Now: multivariate ridge regression in genridge

<!--
The news hook. Development version on GitHub, not CRAN.
- ridge(cbind(Y1, Y2) ~ ..., data, lambda) returns class "mlmridge".
- Honest finding: with a shared lambda, each column of B(lambda) IS the univariate ridge.
  The penalty involves only X. So df, shrinkage factors, VIFs are unchanged.
- What's new is Var(vec B) = Sigma (x) V_lambda (Kronecker): the cross-response
  coefficient ellipses all have Sigma's shape; only size and center change with lambda.
- Figure: faceted traceplot() (all responses), and, if ready, the cross-response ellipses.
- Design lesson: "mlmridge" deliberately does NOT inherit from "ridge" (plan section 10
  audit found inherited methods that would silently give wrong answers). Same
